The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **discrete filtered probability space** is $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, where $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a probability space [[def-probability-measure]], each $\mathcal F_n$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$ [[def-sigma-algebra]], and $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}\subseteq\mathcal F$. The sequence $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a **filtration**. Time starts at zero. Neither completeness nor triviality of $\mathcal F_0$ is required.

Restriction of $P$ to $\mathcal F_n$ has total mass one and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal F_n$ is also such a sequence in $\mathcal F$, with the same union and the same values of $P$. Thus each restriction is a probability measure. This specifies a structure and uses no choice principle. Real-valued processes will be the default.

Assume AC [[def-axiom-of-choice]] for conditional-expectation existence. A **martingale difference sequence** relative to $(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a sequence $(D_n)_{n\ge1}$ of real integrable variables such that $D_n$ is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable and
$$E[D_n\mid\mathcal F_{n-1}]=0\quad\text{a.s. for every }n\ge1.$$
Integrability and adaptedness have the timewise meanings of [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]]. Conditional expectations have the class convention of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]], which is the exact inherited use of AC here. No representative is selected by this definition. There is no $D_0$, and $\mathcal F_0$ need not be trivial or generated by the differences.

Assume AC [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. An integrable adapted real process $X$ [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]] is a **martingale**, **submartingale**, or **supermartingale** when, respectively, for every $n\ge0$,
$$E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=X_n,\qquad E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\ge X_n,\qquad E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\le X_n\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
These are three separate conditions, with the convention that a submartingale has conditional future mean at least its present value. The conditional expectations are the almost-sure classes of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; that supplier inherits AC from its Radon–Nikodym existence proof. The definition itself selects no representative and assumes no completed filtration.

The condition is imposed at each adjacent pair of times. An all-pairs formulation requires a proof. No boundedness or independence is part of this definition, and no trivial or deterministic initial value is imposed.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers ([[def-real-limit]]) converges to a real
number. Together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]], this completes the
construction: $\mathbb{R}$ is a complete totally ordered field.
The proof uses no form of the axiom of choice.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

derivations.claim: Put $Y_n=B_nD_n$. The square-sum bound implies $|B_n|\le\sqrt K$ almost surely, so $Y_n$ is square integrable. Since $B_n$ is $\mathcal F_{n-1}$-measurable, [F2] and [F5] give $E[Y_n\mid\mathcal F_{n-1}]=0$. For $i<j$, [F1] gives $\mathcal F_i\subseteq\mathcal F_{j-1}$, and [F4] gives $E[Y_j\mid\mathcal F_i]=0$. Taking out the bounded $\mathcal F_i$-measurable factor $Y_i$ with [F5], then using expectation preservation [F6], gives $E[Y_iY_j]=0$. Expanding a finite square therefore yields $E\!\left[\left(\sum_{n=N}^{m}Y_n\right)^2\right]=\sum_{n=N}^{m}E[Y_n^2]\le C^2E\!\left[\sum_{n=N}^{m}B_n^2\right].$

Let $R_N=\sum_{n=N}^{\infty}B_n^2$. By [F8], $R_N$ is measurable; the hypothesis gives $0\le R_N\le K$ and $R_N\downarrow0$ almost surely. The constant $K$ is integrable by [F7], so [F9] gives $E[R_N]\to0$.

For finite $m\ge N$, put $S_j=\sum_{n=N}^{j}Y_n$ for $N\le j\le m$, with $S_{N-1}=0$. Each $S_j$ is adapted and integrable; [F2] and [F6] give $E[S_{j+1}\mid\mathcal F_j]=S_j+E[Y_{j+1}\mid\mathcal F_j]=S_j$, so $(S_j)$ is a martingale. Since $S_j$ is $\mathcal F_j$-measurable, [F5] takes it out of the conditional expectation; the MDS identity from step 1.1 gives $E[2S_jY_{j+1}\mid\mathcal F_j]=2S_jE[Y_{j+1}\mid\mathcal F_j]=0$. The conditional square expansion therefore gives $E[S_{j+1}^2\mid\mathcal F_j]=S_j^2+E[Y_{j+1}^2\mid\mathcal F_j]\ge S_j^2,$ so $(S_j^2)$ is a nonnegative submartingale by [F3]. Let $A_j$ be the event that $j$ is the first index in $[N,m]$ with $|S_j|\ge\varepsilon$. These events are disjoint and $A_j\in\mathcal F_j$. Repeated use of the submartingale inequality and [F4] gives $E[S_m^2\mid\mathcal F_j]\ge S_j^2$, hence $E[\mathbf1_{A_j}S_m^2]\ge E[\mathbf1_{A_j}S_j^2]\ge\varepsilon^2P(A_j).$ Summing over $j$ and using $S_m^2\ge0$ gives $P\!\left(\max_{N\le j\le m}|S_j|\ge\varepsilon\right)\le \frac{E[S_m^2]}{\varepsilon^2}\le \frac{C^2E[R_N]}{\varepsilon^2}.$

Since $C^2E[R_N]\to0$, for each integer $r\ge1$ choose the least $N_r>N_{r-1}$ (with $N_0=0$) such that $C^2E[R_{N_r}]\le2^{-4r}$; it exists by [F13]. For finite $m\ge N_r$, step 2.1 with $\varepsilon=2^{-r}$ bounds the event $\max_{N_r\le j\le m}|\sum_{n=N_r}^{j}Y_n|\ge2^{-r}$ by $2^{-2r}$. These events increase with $m$, so [F10] gives the same bound for their union $A_r$ over all $m$. For each $R$, [F11] gives $P(\bigcup_{r\ge R}A_r)\le\sum_{r\ge R}2^{-2r}$, which tends to zero; hence almost surely only finitely many $A_r$ occur. Outside that null event, for every sufficiently large $r$ and all $p\le q$ with $p,q\ge N_r$, the tail sum satisfies $|\sum_{n=p}^{q}Y_n|\le2^{1-r}$. Thus the partial sums are Cauchy.
Completeness [F12] makes the Cauchy sequence of partial sums converge in $\mathbb R$. Since $Y_n=B_nD_n$, this is the asserted convergence of $\sum_{n\ge1}B_nD_n$.

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
[[def-nat-order]], which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]], proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
([[def-equinumerous]]).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \neq 0$, there exists $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n = \sigma(m)$. Equivalently, every natural number is either $0$ or a successor.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathbb{R}$.

- $m$ is a **maximum** (or *greatest element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $s \le m$
  for every $s \in S$.
- $m$ is a **minimum** (or *least element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $m \le s$
  for every $s \in S$.

A set has at most one maximum: if $m_1$ and $m_2$ are both maxima then
$m_1 \in S$ gives $m_1 \le m_2$ and $m_2 \in S$ gives $m_2 \le m_1$, so
$m_1 = m_2$ by antisymmetry of the order, which is immediate from the trichotomy
axiom of an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
The same argument applies to minima, so we may write $\max S$ and $\min S$.

Let $S$ be a finite set, $n := \lvert S\rvert$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]), and
let $a : S \to \mathbb{R}$ or $a : S \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_i$ for $a(i)$.
Choose a bijection $\varphi : n \to S$, which exists because $S \approx n$
([[def-equinumerous]]), and set

$$\sum_{i \in S} a_i := \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)}, \qquad \prod_{i \in S} a_i := \prod_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

the right-hand sides being the iterated operations of [[def-finite-sum]] when the
values are real and of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]] when they are natural.

**Independence of the enumeration, which is the content of the definition.** Let
$\varphi, \psi : n \to S$ be two bijections. Then $\pi := \varphi^{-1} \circ \psi$
is a bijection $n \to n$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and
$a_{\psi(k)} = a_{\varphi(\pi(k))}$ for every $k < n$. Applying
[[lem-finite-sum-permutation-invariance]] to the list $c_k := a_{\varphi(k)}$
gives

$$\sum_{k<n} a_{\psi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_k = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

and identically for products. So the value does not depend on which bijection is
used, and $\sum_{i \in S} a_i$ is a single well-determined element.

**No choice principle is involved.** The definition does not select an
enumeration: it asserts that all enumerations give the same value, and that value
is what the notation names. Only one bijection is ever produced at a time, from a
set already known to be nonempty.

**Three clauses, recorded here because the page uses them constantly.**

**(a) The bridge to the old notation.** Taking $S = n$ and $\varphi = \mathrm{id}_n$,
which is legitimate since $\lvert n\rvert = n$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in n} a_i = \sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad \prod_{i \in n} a_i = \prod_{k<n} a_k .$$

So the new notation **extends** the sum over an initial segment rather than
competing with it, and every law proved for the latter is available for the
former whenever the index set is a natural number.

**(b) Reindexing along a bijection.** If $h : T \to S$ is a bijection of finite
sets, then $\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$, and likewise for
products. Indeed $\lvert T\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = n$ by transport
([[def-finite-cardinality]]), and if $\varphi : n \to S$ is a bijection then
$h^{-1} \circ \varphi : n \to T$ is one, so
$\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{k<n} a_{h(h^{-1}(\varphi(k)))} = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$.

**(c) The empty index set and a constant summand.** $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$,
so $\sum_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 0$ and $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 1$ by
the base clause of the recursion. And for a constant $c$, clause (a) together
with the constant clause of [[lem-nat-finite-sum-laws-and-the-canonical-embedding]]
in $\mathbb{N}$, or clause 2 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] in $\mathbb{R}$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in S} c = \lvert S\rvert \cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{N}), \qquad \sum_{i \in S} c = \iota(\lvert S\rvert)\cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{R}),$$

the second with $\iota$ written out because $\lvert S\rvert$ is a natural number
and not an element of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-canonical-natural]]).

derivations.claim: Fix $s'\in S$. By [F1] and [F2], choose a natural $n$ and a bijection $\phi:\sigma(n)\to A(s')$. The list $u_j=Q(s',\phi(j))$ for $j\in\sigma(n)$ has an attained maximum $m$ by [F3]. Every action $b\in A(s')$ equals $\phi(j)$ for some $j$, so $Q(s',b)\le m$, and the maximum value $m$ is attained by at least one such action.

The maximum value in step 1.1 depends only on the set $\{Q(s',b):b\in A(s')\}$: it belongs to that set and bounds every member. Uniqueness in [F4] therefore makes it independent of the enumeration $\phi$. Hence $\max_{b\in A(s')}Q(s',b)$ is well-defined.

For each $(s,a)\in D$, the bracketed term in the Definition is real by step 2.1, and $S\times\mathcal R$ is finite by [F1]. The finite sum supplied by [F5] is therefore a real number. Thus the displayed formula assigns one real value to every coordinate in $D$ and defines a map $H:\mathbb R^D\to\mathbb R^D$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
[[def-nat-order]], which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]], proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
([[def-equinumerous]]).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let a finite MDP have nonempty state set $S$, and let $\pi$ be a stationary Markov policy. Put $E=S\times(\mathcal R\cup\{0\})$ with its discrete sigma-algebra and define, for $x=(s,\eta)\in E$ and $B\subseteq E$,

$$ K_\pi(x,B)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s) \sum_{\substack{s'\in S\\\rho\in\mathcal R}}1_B(s',\rho)\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

Then $K_\pi$ is a probability kernel on $E$. For each initial state $s\in S$, there is a probability law on $E^{\mathbb N}$ whose coordinate process starts at $(s,0)$ and is a time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K_\pi$ relative to its natural filtration.

Let $S$ and $T$ be finite sets and let $a : S \times T \to \mathbb{R}$, or
$a : S \times T \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_{ij}$ for $a(i,j)$. Then $S \times T$
is finite and

$$\sum_{i \in S}\Big(\sum_{j \in T} a_{ij}\Big) \;=\; \sum_{p \in S \times T} a_p \;=\; \sum_{j \in T}\Big(\sum_{i \in S} a_{ij}\Big),$$

all three sums being the sums over a finite index set of
[[def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set]], carried by [[def-finite-sum]] when the
values are real and by [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]] when they are natural.

**This is not a clause of [[thm-sum-rule]].** That theorem splits one sum along a
partition of *its own* index set; the identity above exchanges the roles of two
*different* index sets, and it is what an argument that counts a set of pairs in
two ways needs. Both outer index sets may be empty, in which case all three
quantities are $0$ (respectively $1$ for the product form of the underlying
recursion), since a sum over the empty index set is the empty sum.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **discrete filtered probability space** is $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, where $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a probability space [[def-probability-measure]], each $\mathcal F_n$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$ [[def-sigma-algebra]], and $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}\subseteq\mathcal F$. The sequence $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a **filtration**. Time starts at zero. Neither completeness nor triviality of $\mathcal F_0$ is required.

Restriction of $P$ to $\mathcal F_n$ has total mass one and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal F_n$ is also such a sequence in $\mathcal F$, with the same union and the same values of $P$. Thus each restriction is a probability measure. This specifies a structure and uses no choice principle. Real-valued processes will be the default.

Assume AC [[def-axiom-of-choice]] for conditional-expectation existence. A **martingale difference sequence** relative to $(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a sequence $(D_n)_{n\ge1}$ of real integrable variables such that $D_n$ is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable and
$$E[D_n\mid\mathcal F_{n-1}]=0\quad\text{a.s. for every }n\ge1.$$
Integrability and adaptedness have the timewise meanings of [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]]. Conditional expectations have the class convention of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]], which is the exact inherited use of AC here. No representative is selected by this definition. There is no $D_0$, and $\mathcal F_0$ need not be trivial or generated by the differences.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0},P)$ be a discrete filtered probability space. Let $(D_n)_{n\ge1}$ be a real martingale-difference sequence relative to the filtration, with $|D_n|\le C$ almost surely for a finite constant $C\ge0$. For each $n\ge1$, let $B_n$ be a real $\mathcal F_{n-1}$-measurable random variable. Suppose that a finite deterministic $K\ge0$ satisfies

$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} B_n^2\le K\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

Then the partial sums $\sum_{n=1}^N B_nD_n$ converge almost surely to a finite real limit.

Let $(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a sequence in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]). For each $N\in\mathbb N$, completeness of $\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[lem-extended-reals-complete]]) gives the tail bounds

$$u_N:=\sup_{k\ge N}a_k,\qquad \ell_N:=\inf_{k\ge N}a_k.$$

The **limit superior** and **limit inferior** of $(a_n)$ are

$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}a_n:=\inf_{N\in\mathbb N}u_N,\qquad \liminf_{n\to\infty}a_n:=\sup_{N\in\mathbb N}\ell_N.$$

All four suprema and infima exist in $\overline{\mathbb R}$, including when some terms are $+\infty$. This definition is therefore distinct from the real-sequence definition: it applies directly to sequences of measure values.

derivations.claim: Fix $i\in I$ and put $B_{n+1}^{(i)}=\mathbf1_{\{I_n=i\}}\alpha_{N_n(i)}(i)$. The indicator and visit count are $\mathcal F_n$-measurable, so $B_{n+1}^{(i)}$ is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable. Each visit to $i$ contributes one term $\alpha_k(i)^2$ to $\sum_{n\ge0}(B_{n+1}^{(i)})^2$, hence this sum is at most $\sum_{k\ge0}\alpha_k(i)^2<\infty$. By [F2], [F4], and the bound on $\xi$, the series $\sum_{n\ge0}B_{n+1}^{(i)}\xi_{n+1}$ converges almost surely. Since $I$ is finite, these convergence events hold simultaneously for all $i$ outside one null set.

Fix an outcome in that full-measure event where all coordinates are visited infinitely often and the iterates are bounded. For a fixed $i$, let $\tau_i(k)$ be the time of the $(k+1)$st update of coordinate $i$, put $z_0=x_0(i)-x^*(i)$ and $z_{k+1}=x_{\tau_i(k)+1}(i)-x^*(i)$, and let $u_k=(T(x_{\tau_i(k)}))(i)-x^*(i)$ and $v_k=\alpha_k(i)\xi_{\tau_i(k)+1}$. Before the $(k+1)$st update, coordinate $i$ still has its value after the first $k$ updates, so the update and $T(x^*)=x^*$ give $z_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_k(i))z_k+\alpha_k(i)u_k+v_k$. By step 1.1, $\sum_{k\ge0}v_k$ converges; put $e_k=\sum_{j\ge k}v_j$, so $e_k\to0$. For $y_k=z_k+e_k$, the identity $e_k=v_k+e_{k+1}$ gives $y_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_k(i))y_k+\alpha_k(i)(u_k+e_k).$

Let $U_i=\limsup_{k\to\infty}|u_k|$, which is finite because the iterates are bounded and $T$ is a contraction. For every $\varepsilon>0$, eventually $|u_k+e_k|\le U_i+2\varepsilon$. Iterating the convex-combination recurrence in step 2.1 from such an index $m$ bounds $|y_k|$ by a vanishing multiple of $|y_m|$ plus $U_i+2\varepsilon$: the coefficient of $|y_m|$ is $\prod_{j=m}^{k-1}(1-\alpha_j(i))$, which tends to zero since $\prod_{j=m}^{k-1}(1-\alpha_j(i))\le\frac{1}{1+\sum_{j=m}^{k-1}\alpha_j(i)}\longrightarrow0.$ Thus $\limsup_k|y_k|\le U_i+2\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and using $e_k\to0$ yields $\limsup_k|z_k|\le U_i$.

Put $E=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\|x_n-x^*\|_\infty$, finite by boundedness. For every $\varepsilon>0$, eventually $\|x_n-x^*\|_\infty\le E+\varepsilon$. Since $\tau_i(k)\to\infty$, contraction gives $|u_k|=|(T(x_{\tau_i(k)}))(i)-(T(x^*))(i)|\le q\|x_{\tau_i(k)}-x^*\|_\infty$, so $U_i\le qE$. Step 3.1 gives $\limsup_k|z_k|\le qE$. Coordinate $i$ is constant between updates; since the number of its updates tends to infinity, its full-time limsup error equals the limsup of the post-update sequence $|z_k|$. Also, for finite $I$, taking a tail supremum commutes with the finite maximum, and the decreasing tail suprema commute with a finite maximum when taking their infimum; hence $E=\max_{i\in I}\limsup_n|x_n(i)-x^*(i)|$. Therefore $E\le qE$, and $0\le q<1$ forces $E=0$. Thus $\|x_n-x^*\|_\infty\to0$ on the full-measure event, proving almost-sure convergence.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

For a finite MDP and a discount $0\le\gamma<1$, define the **Bellman optimality operator** $T^*:\mathbb R^S\to\mathbb R^S$ by

$$ (T^*V)(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]\qquad(s\in S). $$

The maximum exists because each $A(s)$ is finite and nonempty. If $S=\emptyset$, this is the unique map from $\mathbb R^S$ to itself.

Let a finite MDP and a discount $0\le\gamma<1$ be fixed. For every stationary policy $\pi$ and all $V,W\in\mathbb R^S$,

$$ \|T^\pi V-T^\pi W\|_\infty\le\gamma\|V-W\|_\infty. $$

The Bellman optimality operator satisfies the same inequality. Each of $T^\pi$ and $T^*$ has exactly one fixed point in $\mathbb R^S$. The contraction constant is the nonnegative number $\gamma$.

Let a finite MDP have nonempty finite state set $S$ and let $0\le\gamma<1$. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$ and $\mathbb R^D$ for the real functions on $D$. The **optimal action-value Bellman operator** $H:\mathbb R^D\to\mathbb R^D$ is

$$
(HQ)(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\left[\rho+\gamma\max_{b\in A(s')}Q(s',b)\right]\qquad ((s,a)\in D).
$$

Each maximum is attained because every $A(s')$ is finite and nonempty.

**Inputs:** A finite MDP with nonempty finite state set $S$, finite nonempty action sets $A(s)$, finite reward alphabet $\mathcal R$, and discount $0\le\gamma<1$; an initial state $S_0\in S$; a behavior rule that selects a legal action using the interaction history available at time $n$; an initial table $Q_0\in\mathbb R^D$; and a step-size rule that, before observing the next reward and state, supplies $\alpha_n(S_n,A_n)\in[0,1]$ from the history and selected pair. A deterministic per-pair schedule $\alpha_k(s,a)\in[0,1]$ based on the number of previous visits to $(s,a)$ is a special case. The interaction must, conditional on its history and the selected pair $(S_n,A_n)$, draw $(S_{n+1},R_{n+1})$ with joint mass $p(s',\rho\mid S_n,A_n)$.

**Output:** The action-value table after every interaction, $(Q_n)_{n\ge0}$; a finite run outputs its current table $Q_n$.

Initialize $Q=Q_0$. For each $n=0,1,2,\ldots$, select $A_n$ by the behavior rule, obtain $\alpha_n(S_n,A_n)$ from the step-size rule, and observe $(R_{n+1},S_{n+1})$. Compute

$$
\delta_n=R_{n+1}+\gamma\max_{b\in A(S_{n+1})}Q_n(S_{n+1},b)-Q_n(S_n,A_n),
$$

then update only the visited coordinate by

$$
Q_{n+1}(S_n,A_n)=Q_n(S_n,A_n)+\alpha_n(S_n,A_n)\delta_n.
$$

Leave every other coordinate unchanged, set the current table to $Q_{n+1}$, and set the current state to $S_{n+1}$. The target uses the greedy maximum even when the behavior rule explores, so this is off-policy and uses no importance-sampling ratio. The procedure makes no convergence claim; convergence requires additional hypotheses not imposed here.

A **discrete filtered probability space** is $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, where $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a probability space [[def-probability-measure]], each $\mathcal F_n$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$ [[def-sigma-algebra]], and $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}\subseteq\mathcal F$. The sequence $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a **filtration**. Time starts at zero. Neither completeness nor triviality of $\mathcal F_0$ is required.

Restriction of $P$ to $\mathcal F_n$ has total mass one and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal F_n$ is also such a sequence in $\mathcal F$, with the same union and the same values of $P$. Thus each restriction is a probability measure. This specifies a structure and uses no choice principle. Real-valued processes will be the default.

Assume AC [[def-axiom-of-choice]] for conditional-expectation existence. A **martingale difference sequence** relative to $(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a sequence $(D_n)_{n\ge1}$ of real integrable variables such that $D_n$ is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable and
$$E[D_n\mid\mathcal F_{n-1}]=0\quad\text{a.s. for every }n\ge1.$$
Integrability and adaptedness have the timewise meanings of [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]]. Conditional expectations have the class convention of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]], which is the exact inherited use of AC here. No representative is selected by this definition. There is no $D_0$, and $\mathcal F_0$ need not be trivial or generated by the differences.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $I$ be a nonempty finite set and put $\|x\|_\infty=\max_{i\in I}|x(i)|$ for $x\in\mathbb R^I$. Let $T:\mathbb R^I\to\mathbb R^I$ satisfy

$$\|T(x)-T(y)\|_\infty\le q\|x-y\|_\infty\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^I)$$

for a fixed $0\le q<1$, and let $x^*\in\mathbb R^I$ satisfy $T(x^*)=x^*$. On a discrete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0},P)$, let $x_0\in\mathbb R^I$ be deterministic, let $I_n\in I$ be $\mathcal F_n$-measurable, and define $N_n(i)=\#\{k<n:I_k=i\}$. For each $i\in I$, let $\alpha_k(i)$ be deterministic with $0\le\alpha_k(i)\le1$, $\sum_{k\ge0}\alpha_k(i)=\infty$, and $\sum_{k\ge0}\alpha_k(i)^2<\infty$. Let $(\xi_{n+1})_{n\ge0}$ be a bounded martingale-difference sequence relative to the filtration. Update

$$x_{n+1}(i)=x_n(i)+\mathbf1_{\{I_n=i\}}\alpha_{N_n(i)}(i)\big((T(x_n))(i)-x_n(i)+\xi_{n+1}\big)\qquad(i\in I).$$

If every $i\in I$ is selected infinitely often almost surely and the iterates $x_n$ are bounded almost surely, then $x_n\to x^*$ almost surely in $\|\cdot\|_\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let a finite MDP have nonempty finite state set $S$ and discount $0\le\gamma<1$, and let $T^*$ be its Bellman optimality operator. For a fixed initial pair $(s,a)\in D$, an **admissible continuation** is any discrete filtered process $(S_n,A_n,R_{n+1})_{n\ge0}$ on a probability space such that $(S_0,A_0)=(s,a)$ almost surely, $S_n,S_{n+1}\in S$, $A_n\in A(S_n)$, $R_{n+1}\in\mathcal R$ almost surely, $(S_n,A_n)$ is measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_n$, $R_{n+1}$ and $S_{n+1}$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_{n+1}$, and

$$ E[\mathbf1_{\{S_{n+1}=s',\,R_{n+1}=\rho\}}\mid\mathcal F_n]=p(s',\rho\mid S_n,A_n) $$

almost surely for every $n\ge0$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$. Its discounted return is $G=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\gamma^nR_{n+1}$. Let $V^*$ be the unique fixed point of $T^*$ and define $Q_{\mathrm{opt}}(s,a)$ as the supremum of $E[G]$ over all admissible continuations from $(s,a)$. Then this supremum is finite and attained by a continuation that, after the prescribed initial action, always chooses an action maximizing $r(s',b)+\gamma\sum_{u\in S}P(u\mid s',b)V^*(u)$ at the current state $s'$. In particular,

$$ Q_{\mathrm{opt}}(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)[\rho+\gamma V^*(s')]. $$

Any other fixed point $Q$ would then satisfy $\|Q-Q^\dagger\|_\infty\le\gamma\|Q-Q^\dagger\|_\infty$; since $\gamma<1$, this forces $Q=Q^\dagger$. By [F10], this fixed point is the pointwise maximal expected discounted return from each initial state-action pair and is attained by a greedy stationary continuation, so it is the optimal action-value function $Q^*$ in the Statement.

Put $C=\max\{\|Q_0\|_\infty,M/(1-\gamma)\}$. Then $M+\gamma C\le C$. If $\|Q_n\|_\infty\le C$, the sampled target $Y_{n+1}=R_{n+1}+\gamma\max_bQ_n(S_{n+1},b)$ lies in $[-M-\gamma C,M+\gamma C]\subseteq[-C,C]$. The update is a convex combination of $Q_n(I_n)$ and $Y_{n+1}$ because $0\le\alpha_{N_n(I_n)}(I_n)\le1$; hence induction gives $\|Q_n\|_\infty\le C$ for every $n$.

By induction from deterministic $Q_0$, the update and the observation measurability in the Statement make $Q_n$ $\mathcal F_n$-measurable. Define $\xi_{n+1}=Y_{n+1}-(HQ_n)(I_n)$. Expand $Y_{n+1}$ as a finite sum over $s'\in S$ and $\rho\in\mathcal R$ using the indicators of $(S_{n+1},R_{n+1})=(s',\rho)$. Since $Q_n$ and $I_n$ are $\mathcal F_n$-measurable, the conditional transition-reward identity in the Statement, linearity, and taking out known factors [F7]–[F8] give $E[Y_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=(HQ_n)(I_n)$. Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

**Inputs:** A finite MDP with nonempty finite state set $S$, finite nonempty action sets $A(s)$, finite reward alphabet $\mathcal R$, and discount $0\le\gamma<1$; an initial state $S_0\in S$; a behavior rule that selects a legal action using the interaction history available at time $n$; an initial table $Q_0\in\mathbb R^D$; and a step-size rule that, before observing the next reward and state, supplies $\alpha_n(S_n,A_n)\in[0,1]$ from the history and selected pair. A deterministic per-pair schedule $\alpha_k(s,a)\in[0,1]$ based on the number of previous visits to $(s,a)$ is a special case. The interaction must, conditional on its history and the selected pair $(S_n,A_n)$, draw $(S_{n+1},R_{n+1})$ with joint mass $p(s',\rho\mid S_n,A_n)$.

**Output:** The action-value table after every interaction, $(Q_n)_{n\ge0}$; a finite run outputs its current table $Q_n$.

Initialize $Q=Q_0$. For each $n=0,1,2,\ldots$, select $A_n$ by the behavior rule, obtain $\alpha_n(S_n,A_n)$ from the step-size rule, and observe $(R_{n+1},S_{n+1})$. Compute

$$
\delta_n=R_{n+1}+\gamma\max_{b\in A(S_{n+1})}Q_n(S_{n+1},b)-Q_n(S_n,A_n),
$$

then update only the visited coordinate by

$$
Q_{n+1}(S_n,A_n)=Q_n(S_n,A_n)+\alpha_n(S_n,A_n)\delta_n.
$$

Leave every other coordinate unchanged, set the current table to $Q_{n+1}$, and set the current state to $S_{n+1}$. The target uses the greedy maximum even when the behavior rule explores, so this is off-policy and uses no importance-sampling ratio. The procedure makes no convergence claim; convergence requires additional hypotheses not imposed here.

Let a finite MDP have nonempty finite state set $S$ and let $0\le\gamma<1$. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$ and $\mathbb R^D$ for the real functions on $D$. The **optimal action-value Bellman operator** $H:\mathbb R^D\to\mathbb R^D$ is

$$
(HQ)(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\left[\rho+\gamma\max_{b\in A(s')}Q(s',b)\right]\qquad ((s,a)\in D).
$$

Each maximum is attained because every $A(s')$ is finite and nonempty.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

For a stationary policy $\sigma$, an episode starting from $s$ ends at its first hitting time $T=\inf\{n\ge0:S_n\in S_\dagger\}$; require $T<\infty$ almost surely under every policy used. The return from time $t<T$ is

$$
G_t=\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}\gamma^{k-t}R_{k+1},
$$

and $G_T=0$. This equals the infinite discounted return of the absorbing extension, whose state value is $V^\sigma(s)=\mathbb E_{\sigma,s}[G_0]$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

A **discrete filtered probability space** is $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, where $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a probability space [[def-probability-measure]], each $\mathcal F_n$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$ [[def-sigma-algebra]], and $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}\subseteq\mathcal F$. The sequence $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a **filtration**. Time starts at zero. Neither completeness nor triviality of $\mathcal F_0$ is required.

Restriction of $P$ to $\mathcal F_n$ has total mass one and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal F_n$ is also such a sequence in $\mathcal F$, with the same union and the same values of $P$. Thus each restriction is a probability measure. This specifies a structure and uses no choice principle. Real-valued processes will be the default.

Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

$$ (T^*V)(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]\qquad(s\in S). $$

The maximum exists because each $A(s)$ is finite and nonempty. If $S=\emptyset$, this is the unique map from $\mathbb R^S$ to itself.

For a finite MDP, a discount $0\le\gamma<1$, and a stationary Markov policy $\pi$, define the **policy Bellman operator** $T^\pi:\mathbb R^S\to\mathbb R^S$ by

$$ (T^\pi V)(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]\qquad(s\in S). $$

If $S=\emptyset$, this is the unique map from $\mathbb R^S$ to itself.

Let a finite MDP and a discount $0\le\gamma<1$ be fixed. For every stationary policy $\pi$ and all $V,W\in\mathbb R^S$,

$$ \|T^\pi V-T^\pi W\|_\infty\le\gamma\|V-W\|_\infty. $$

The Bellman optimality operator satisfies the same inequality. Each of $T^\pi$ and $T^*$ has exactly one fixed point in $\mathbb R^S$. The contraction constant is the nonnegative number $\gamma$.

The **discounted return** is

$$ G_t=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\gamma^jR_{t+j+1}, $$

and the **state value under $\pi$** is $V^\pi(s)=\mathbb E_{\pi,s}[G_0]$, where $\mathbb E_{\pi,s}$ is expectation under that start-state law. If $S=\emptyset$, $V^\pi$ is the unique empty function. The definition concerns discounted infinite-horizon tasks; average-reward and undiscounted continuing models, and improper episodic tasks, are outside its scope.

The coordinate $0$ in $X_0=(s,0)$ is only a dummy initial reward; the chain's one-step kernel emits rewards in $\mathcal R$. If $S=\emptyset$, this is the equality of the unique empty functions and no choice axiom is needed. If $S\ne\emptyset$, assume the Axiom of Choice for the path-law definition of $V^\pi$.

In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and

$$Z=\{(s,a,r,s'):s\in S,\ a\in A(s),\ r\in\mathcal R,\ s'\in S\}$$

$$

for each feasible finite state-reward path $(s_0,r_1,s_1,\ldots,r_m,s_m)$.

Let $M\ge0$, $0\le\gamma<1$, and let $(\rho_j)_{j\ge1}$ be any real sequence with $|\rho_j|\le M$. Then the series

$$ \sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\gamma^j\rho_{j+1} $$

converges absolutely. Every partial sum and the limit satisfy

$$ \left|\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\gamma^j\rho_{j+1}\right|\le\frac{M}{1-\gamma}, \qquad |G|\le\frac{M}{1-\gamma}. $$

$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $A\in\mathcal F$.
Then the indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
[[def-nat-order]], which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]], proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
([[def-equinumerous]]).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

Let $\mathbb{N} = \omega$ be the von Neumann naturals, with $0 = \varnothing$ and
$\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and let $\le$ and $<$ be
the order defined additively by $m \le n \iff \exists k \in \mathbb{N}\ (m + k = n)$
and $m < n \iff (m \le n$ and $m \ne n)$ ([[def-nat-order]]). Then $\mathbb{N}$ is
a **transitive set**: every element of a natural number is itself a natural
number. Moreover, for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$:

1. $m < n \iff m \in n$;
2. $m \le n \iff m \subseteq n$;
3. $n < \sigma(n)$, and $m < \sigma(n) \iff m \le n$;
4. $0 \le n$, and $0 \in n$ whenever $n \ne 0$.

Consequently $n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\}$ for every $n$: a natural
number is exactly the set of the naturals below it.

**Why this is proved here.** [[def-nat-order]] defines the order additively and
records the identification with membership only as an orienting remark, without
proof. The countability arguments on this page use that identification as a
working fact, so it is established here, from the additive order and induction
alone. Nothing below uses ordinals or any later material.
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \neq 0$, there exists $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n = \sigma(m)$. Equivalently, every natural number is either $0$ or a successor.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathbb{R}$.

- $m$ is a **maximum** (or *greatest element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $s \le m$
  for every $s \in S$.
- $m$ is a **minimum** (or *least element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $m \le s$
  for every $s \in S$.

A set has at most one maximum: if $m_1$ and $m_2$ are both maxima then
$m_1 \in S$ gives $m_1 \le m_2$ and $m_2 \in S$ gives $m_2 \le m_1$, so
$m_1 = m_2$ by antisymmetry of the order, which is immediate from the trichotomy
axiom of an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
The same argument applies to minima, so we may write $\max S$ and $\min S$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: The unique fixed point $V^*$ exists by [F6]. Let $B=\|V^*\|_\infty$, which is finite because $S$ is finite. Fix $s\in S$ and enumerate $A(s)=\{a_0,\ldots,a_n\}$ using [F1] and [F14]. For $u_j=r(s,a_j)+\gamma\sum_xP(x\mid s,a_j)V^*(x)$, [F15] gives an attained list maximum; because the list enumerates all actions, its maximum is exactly the maximum in [F4], independent of the enumeration by uniqueness in [F15]. For each $j$, expanding $r$ and $P$ by [F1] gives $u_j=\sum_{x,\rho}p(x,\rho\mid s,a_j)[\rho+\gamma V^*(x)]$. The triangle inequality, $|\rho|\le M$, and the probability-mass identity give $|u_j|\le M+\gamma B$. Since the maximum is one of the list entries, $|(T^*V^*)(s)|\le M+\gamma B$. As $s$ was arbitrary, $B=\|T^*V^*\|_\infty\le M+\gamma B$. Since $1-\gamma>0$, $B\le M/(1-\gamma)$.

Fix any admissible continuation from $(s,a)$. For each $n\ge1$, expand $R_{n+1}+\gamma V^*(S_{n+1})$ as the finite sum $\sum_{s',\rho}(\rho+\gamma V^*(s'))\mathbf1_{\{S_{n+1}=s',R_{n+1}=\rho\}}$. These variables are bounded by [F1] and step 1.1, so they are integrable. Conditional linearity and the transition-reward identity in the definition give $E[R_{n+1}+\gamma V^*(S_{n+1})\mid\mathcal F_n]=\sum_{s',\rho}p(s',\rho\mid S_n,A_n)[\rho+\gamma V^*(s')]$. The right side is the one-step action value of the measurable current action $A_n$, so it is at most $(T^*V^*)(S_n)=V^*(S_n)$ by [F4] and the fixed-point identity.

The attained list maximum argument in step 1.1 makes the maximizing-action set nonempty at every state. By [A1], choose one such action at every state and call the resulting deterministic stationary policy $\pi^*$. The definitions [F4]–[F5] and $T^*V^*=V^*$ give $T^{\pi^*}V^*=V^*$. By [F6] this is the unique fixed point of $T^{\pi^*}$, while [F8] gives $T^{\pi^*}V^{\pi^*}=V^{\pi^*}$; hence $V^{\pi^*}=V^*$.

Apply order and expectation preservation from [F3] to the conditional inequality in step 2.1, multiply by the nonnegative scalar $\gamma^n$, and sum for $n=1,\ldots,N$. The intermediate state-value terms cancel, giving $\sum_{n=1}^N\gamma^nE[R_{n+1}]+\gamma^{N+1}E[V^*(S_{N+1})]\le\gamma E[V^*(S_1)]$. The initial transition law gives $E[R_1+\gamma V^*(S_1)]=\sum_{s',\rho}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)[\rho+\gamma V^*(s')]=:Q^\dagger(s,a)$. Since $|E[V^*(S_{N+1})]|\le B$ by step 1.1 and [F13], it follows that $E[\sum_{n=0}^N\gamma^nR_{n+1}]\le Q^\dagger(s,a)+\gamma^{N+1}B$.

Write $G_N=\sum_{n=0}^N\gamma^nR_{n+1}$. Each $G_N$ is measurable because it is a finite sum of measurable rewards, and [F11] gives pointwise convergence to $G$ and the bound $|G_N|\le M/(1-\gamma)$. Thus $G$ is measurable by [F17]; the constant bound is integrable by [F13], so [F12] gives $E[G_N]\to E[G]$. Also $\gamma^{N+1}B\to0$ by [F16]. Passing to the limit in the upper bound of step 3.1 shows $E[G]\le Q^\dagger(s,a)$. The continuation was arbitrary, so $Q_{\mathrm{opt}}(s,a)\le Q^\dagger(s,a)$.

Construct a continuation with initial pair $(s,a)$ and thereafter action $\pi^*(S_{n+1})$ following each transition. Take $E_0=D$ and $E_{n+1}=\mathcal R\times D$ with their discrete sigma-algebras, initial law concentrated at $(s,a)$, and history kernels $K_n(h,B)=\sum_{s',\rho}p(s',\rho\mid s_n,a_n)\mathbf1_B(\rho,(s',\pi^*(s')))$ for every measurable $B\subseteq E_{n+1}$, where $(s_n,a_n)$ is the last pair in $h$. For disjoint sets $B_j\subseteq E_{n+1}$, their preimages $\{(s',\rho):(\rho,(s',\pi^*(s')))\in B_j\}$ are disjoint subsets of the finite set $S\times\mathcal R$, so only finitely many are nonempty and the finite mass formula is countably additive; its total mass is one by [F1]. It is measurable in $h$ because it is a finite sum of functions of the current-pair coordinate projection, which is measurable by [F18]. Thus each $K_n$ is a probability kernel by [F19], and [F9] gives a path law with these prefix products. Set $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_0,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)$, where $X_0=(S_0,A_0)$ and $Y_j=(R_j,(S_j,A_j))$. The coordinate projections make current pairs measurable at time $n$ and next observations measurable at time $n+1$ by [F18]. The finite history-coordinate set is finite by [F20], so each atom of $\mathcal F_n$ fixes a finite history. On a positive-mass atom ending at $(s_n,a_n)$, the prefix product in [F9] shows that extending it by reward $\rho$, state $s'$, and next action $\pi^*(s')$ has conditional probability $p(s',\rho\mid s_n,a_n)$; all other next-action extensions have conditional probability zero. Hence this process is admissible. By the product form of the finite-prefix probabilities, after the first transition its conditional continuation from $S_1=s'$ has the stationary-policy prefix laws in [F10], so [F7] identifies its conditional expected discounted tail as $V^{\pi^*}(s')$. The expectation convergence proved for every admissible continuation in step 4.1 passes this prefix identity to the infinite return. Therefore $E[G]=\sum_{s',\rho}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)[\rho+\gamma V^{\pi^*}(s')]=Q^\dagger(s,a)$ by step 2.2. This admissible continuation attains the upper bound, so $Q_{\mathrm{opt}}(s,a)=Q^\dagger(s,a)$ and the supremum is a finite maximum.
Since $(s,a)$ was arbitrary, the formula and finite attainment claim hold on all of $D$.
